title: The Future Feature

scenario.situation: A cancellation model uses a refund_issued field and scores AUC 0.98. The team is excited and wants to ship it to production immediately.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team believes the model is genuinely excellent and that refund_issued is a strong early signal of customer intent to cancel.
scenario.question: Is this model actually deployable, or is something artificially inflating its performance?

decisions.prompt: The team wants to move fast. How do you investigate before signing off on deployment?

options.label: Validate on a held-out test set
options.detail: Split off a random 20% test set and confirm AUC holds there too.
options.consequence: AUC is 0.97 on the holdout — still looks great. The data leak travels with the split because refund_issued is populated the same way everywhere; a random split cannot expose a temporal integrity problem.
options.divergenceCost: Validated the artifact of the leak, not the model's real predictive power.

options.label: Audit feature temporality
options.detail: For each feature, check whether its value could be known at the moment a prediction would be made in production — before any outcome is recorded.
options.consequence: The audit immediately flags refund_issued: it is only written to the database after a cancellation is confirmed. In production the field would be NULL at prediction time. You've found the real problem before a single bad prediction ships.

options.label: Run SHAP feature importances
options.detail: Compute SHAP values to understand which features drive the predictions.
options.consequence: SHAP correctly shows refund_issued as the dominant driver — but the output is framed as 'the model relies on a strong signal,' not as a red flag. Without a temporality lens, SHAP confirms the leak rather than exposing it.
options.divergenceCost: Interpreted a leak's dominance as a feature strength rather than a warning.

options.label: Compare AUC to industry benchmarks
options.detail: Research published cancellation model AUCs to see if 0.98 is unusual.
options.consequence: You note 0.98 is suspiciously high, but benchmarks alone give no diagnostic path. The team dismisses it as Coverly having 'richer data,' and the deployment conversation restarts.
options.divergenceCost: Raised a flag without a mechanism to trace and confirm the root cause.

decisions.prompt: You suspect refund_issued may be leaking the label. Which comparison makes the case most clearly to the team?

artifact.title: Model AUC by feature set — full training data
artifact.caption: AUC scores across feature subsets. The single field refund_issued nearly matches the full model — but is that signal or a shortcut?

options.label: AUC on the full feature set vs. behavioral-only subset
options.detail: Compare overall model AUC to a version trained without refund_issued but still on the same historical data.
options.consequence: AUC drops from 0.98 to 0.71 when refund_issued is removed — a dramatic gap — but the team argues the field is simply 'predictive' and proposes engineering a proxy for it. The temporal problem isn't obviously visible in this comparison alone.
options.divergenceCost: Showed the performance gap without proving the field is unavailable at prediction time.

options.label: AUC on a point-in-time holdout where refund_issued is NULL for all rows
options.detail: Reconstruct a validation set using only feature values that existed before the cancellation event timestamp, forcing refund_issued to its true production state (NULL).
options.consequence: With refund_issued forced to NULL — its real production value — AUC collapses to 0.72 and matches behavioral-only performance. The chart makes the mechanism undeniable: the model was memorizing the outcome label disguised as a feature.

artifact.title: Model AUC under point-in-time correctness (refund_issued = NULL at prediction time)
artifact.caption: When refund_issued is forced to its true production state, AUC falls to 0.72 — indistinguishable from behavioral features alone. The 0.98 was the outcome masquerading as a predictor.

decisions.prompt: Point-in-time validation collapses AUC to 0.72. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The model is broken — refund_issued is the label. Scrap it and start over."
options.detail: Declare the model invalid and halt the project.
options.consequence: The team hears 'six weeks of work is worthless' and pushes back hard. Without a constructive path forward, the conversation stalls — and a manager may override you to ship anyway, rationalizing that '0.72 is still decent.'
options.divergenceCost: Delivered the finding without a remediation path, inviting stakeholder resistance.

options.label: "refund_issued is populated post-cancellation, so it leaks the label. The real AUC is ~0.72. Let's retrain on point-in-time features and benchmark that honestly before any deployment decision."
options.detail: Name the mechanism, show the corrected metric, and propose the next step.
options.consequence: You've named the exact mechanism (post-outcome population), quantified the real performance, and given the team a concrete remediation — retrain with a point-in-time feature set and re-evaluate. The project continues on honest footing.

insight: A 0.98 AUC was not model excellence — it was the outcome label recycled as an input feature. refund_issued is only written to the database after a cancellation is recorded, so the model learned to read the answer key. The lesson is point-in-time correctness: every feature value used in training must reflect what was knowable at the moment a real prediction would fire, not what was recorded afterward. Enforcing this discipline — and validating on a temporally reconstructed holdout — is the only way to distinguish genuine signal from future leakage.
